articles.title: Coordenadores de Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro no GloboNews Debate | G1
articles.standfirst: Edinho Silva e Rogério Marinho vão discutir as estratégias dos candidatos na reta final da disputa pela Presidência da República.
articles.summary: O GloboNews Debate recebe Edinho Silva e Rogério Marinho para analisar as táticas das campanhas de Lula e Bolsonaro nesta reta final das eleições.
articles.body:
GloboNews Debate recebe Edinho Silva e Rogério Marinho. — Foto: Reprodução/GloboNews

O GloboNews Debate recebe nesta segunda-feira (19), às 18h20, Edinho Silva, coordenador da campanha do presidente Lula (PT), e Rogério Marinho, coordenador da campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL).

Com mediação da jornalista Julia Duailibi, o programa vai discutir as estratégias das duas campanhas na reta final das eleições presidenciais.

O debate será exibido no Edição das 18h, na GloboNews, e também terá transmissão no g1 .

articles.title: O que pesquisas qualitativas dizem sobre Lula e Flávio no debate e como isso vai refletir nas campanhas | G1
articles.body:
Candidatos Flávio Bolsonaro e Lula participam de debate da Band antes do 2º turno das eleições. — Foto: REUTERS/Jean Carniel

As campanhas de desconstrução ficaram em evidência no debate da Band neste domingo (18) . O objetivo foi aumentar a rejeição do adversário , mostram pesquisas qualitativas. Isso gera um efeito colateral do desencantamento do eleitor. Ao invés de um debate propositivo, aconteceu o contrário.

Parecia que o segundo turno seria pautado de forma diferente, com soluções mais concretas para o futuro. Mas diante de uma disputa muito acirrada, com um cenário de indefinição, a estratégia mudou.

Ao invés de propostas, acusações. Quem perdeu foi eleitor, segundo aferiu pesquisas em grupos de debates. Principalmente aquele eleitor que está indefinido ou não foi votar no primeiro turno.

Questões como o ajuste fiscal não foram aprofundadas. Os candidatos evitaram falar de temas necessários que são impopulares.

A Quaest foi um dos institutos que realizaram pesquisas qualitativas.

Os resultados apontaram Flávio Bolsonaro como mais seguro, direto e claro. Mas, os entrevistados perceberam que ele fugiu de perguntas feitas pro Lula e que evitou abordar temas sobre os quais parecia menos preparado.

Já Lula foi visto como muito preparado para tratar de saúde, mas com respostas, em geral, confusas, carregadas de números e difíceis de acompanhar.

O debate na Band foi um teste para a semana final nas campanhas eleitorais de Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro. Este foi o primeiro encontro entre os dois candidatos nestas eleições. As duas campanhas fizeram grupos de pesquisa qualitativa durante o programa.

O consenso é de que os dois candidatos tiveram dificuldade de atingir eleitores indecisos e não-alinhados. Os pontos positivos e negativos serão trabalhados pelas equipes antes do debate decisivo da TV Globo na sexta-feira (23).

O grupo analisado pela campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) apontou que Lula estava muito nervoso e irritado durante o debate. E que o presidente teria se atrapalhado na tentativa de explicar suas propostas.

Por outro lado, a pesquisa apontou que a postura de Flávio Bolsonaro de se posicionar atrás da câmera durante as falas de Lula passou a percepção de um excesso de ironia e de arrogância por parte do candidato. E que ele precisa ser mais didático na explicação das propostas que está defendendo.

Os resultados da pesquisa encomendada pela campanha de Lula (PT) são semelhantes.

Os eleitores que participaram do grupo focal apontaram que Lula estava cansado e irritado, que não deu respostas diretas às acusações e que não conseguiu explicar suas propostas.

Em relação a Flávio Bolsonaro, o grupo analisado apontou que a postura do candidato foi artificial, mecanizada e excessivamente treinada. A falta de respostas às perguntas feitas por Lula também foram pontuadas pelos entrevistados.

As pesquisas encomendadas pelas campanhas deram pistas sobre temas que deverão ser abordados pelos candidatos nesta reta final.

A equipe de Lula aposta no desafio feito pelo presidente da quebra dos sigilos telefônico e bancário. Enquanto a campanha de Flávio deve abordar a fala de Lula que se referiu ao oponente como "malandro carioca".

Durante uma troca de acusações no debate, Lula desafiou Flávio a quebrar espontaneamente seus sigilos telefônico e bancário "para saber quem é ladrão". O desafio foi bem recebido na pesquisa qualitativa. E o corte desse trecho já começou a ser explorado pela campanha de Lula na linha do ditado popular "quem não deve, não teme".

Em outra troca de acusações, Lula disse que Flávio é um "malandro carioca". A fala começou a ser explorada pela campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro e por seus auxiliares. O líder do PL na Câmara, deputado Sóstenes Cavalcante (PL-RJ), já gravou vídeo defendendo os nascidos no Rio de Janeiro e considerando a fala como preconceituosa.

articles.title: TREs dizem que mudanças de locais de votação são 'excepcionais' e número é menor que em 2022 | G1
articles.standfirst: Presidentes dos tribunais regionais afirmam que dados ainda estão sendo atualizados e que alterações ocorrem em casos como problemas de infraestrutura, eventos climáticos e questões de segurança.
articles.summary: Presidentes dos tribunais regionais afirmam que dados ainda estão sendo atualizados e que alterações ocorrem em casos como problemas de infraestrutura, eventos climáticos e questões de segurança.
articles.body:
Os presidentes dos Tribunais Regionais Eleitorais (TREs) assinaram, nesta segunda-feira (19), uma nota conjunta afirmando que a prioridade da Justiça Eleitoral é não alterar o local de votação entre o primeiro e segundo turno das eleições.

Ainda segundo a nota, o número de seções impactadas pela mudança é bem menor do que em 2022 e ainda há uma atualização do sistema para verificar quais eleitores de fato, serão afetados ( entenda mais abaixo ).

O texto enviado ao presidente do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), Kassio Nunes Marques, garante que haverá ampla divulgação das mudanças , mas também pede a colaboração e atenção do eleitor.

Entre sexta (16) e sábado (17), o sistema da Justiça Eleitoral indicava que mais de 4 mil seções tiveram os locais de votação para o segundo turno alterados . Esse número, contudo, sofreu um série de atualizações ao longo do fim de semana e continua mudando.

Na manhã desta segunda (19), o sistema indicava que a mudança seria de 1.106 locais.

No início da tarde, o TSE registra a alteração de 554 locais de votação em 22 estados , que juntos somam 163,6 mil eleitores.

Agora, são 444 seções eleitorais em que houve alteração do local de votação do primeiro para o segundo turno.

A definição sobre a alteração do local ocorre pelo TREs, de forma excepcional, sem participação do TSE.

"É de competência dos Tribunais Regionais Eleitorais alterar, apenas quando absolutamente necessário, os locais de votação. O Tribunal Superior Eleitoral – TSE não tem ingerência alguma sobre essas alterações", diz a nota do Colégio de Presidentes dos Tribunais Regionais Eleitorais.

O texto afirma que a medida é adotada apenas em situações extraordinárias, como ocorrência de situações climáticas extremas, problemas ocultos na infraestrutura dos prédios usados como locais de votação e questões de segurança pública.

"Os principais motivos que levam os Tribunais Regionais Eleitorais – TREs a realizar essas alterações são sempre extraordinários e estão relacionados à ocorrência de situações climáticas extremas, a problemas não identificados previamente na infraestrutura dos prédios utilizados como locais de votação e a questões de segurança pública. Os dados são encaminhados pelos cartórios eleitorais por meio do sistema Elo para divulgação pelo TSE", diz outro trecho.

Seções eleitorais vão mudar de local em Palmas — Foto: Reprodução/TV Anhanguera

De acordo com os TREs, em 2022, foram 5.822 locais de votação alterados em todo o país. "Neste ano, mesmo com o advento do Super El Niño, os dados disponíveis até o momento indicam uma redução expressiva em relação a esse total".

A nota afirma ainda que "a diretriz seguida à risca pelos tribunais é, sempre que possível, não alterar o local de votação entre os turnos".

A Justiça Eleitoral afirma que a queda nas alterações não envolve nenhum erro no sistema, mas ocorre a partir das providências adotadas pelas próprias zonas eleitorais e atualização realizada.

"O principal ponto diz respeito às alocações provisórias realizadas em caráter emergencial para o primeiro turno, em razão de situações que impediram a utilização dos locais originalmente previstos. Como essas alocações são temporárias, após o primeiro turno as seções retornam automaticamente aos locais de origem. Para que permaneçam no mesmo local utilizado no primeiro turno, as zonas eleitorais precisam importar essas alocações também para o segundo turno", diz o TSE.

Ainda de acordo com o tribunal, "enquanto essa providência não é realizada, o sistema identifica uma alteração de local de votação entre os turnos, pois a seção consta provisoriamente em um local no primeiro turno e retorna ao local de origem no segundo. É justamente a conclusão desses procedimentos que explica boa parte da redução dos quantitativos divulgados".

Mudanças de locais de votação entre os turnos sempre ocorreram e são regularmente divulgadas pelo TSE, sendo que nas eleições gerais de 2014, 2018 e 2022, a média de seções eleitorais com alterações foi de 0,69% e, neste ano, esse percentual está em 0,38% — abaixo da média histórica, e ainda poderá ser atualizado.

➡️O eleitor pode checar seu local de votação no aplicativo e-Título, nos portais da Justiça Eleitoral (TSE e TREs), acessando a página do "Autoatendimento Eleitoral" e consultando a opção “onde votar”.

Até o dia da realização do segundo turno, cada um dos 27 Tribunais Regionais Eleitorais divulgará, por todos os meios de comunicação disponíveis, os locais de votação eventualmente modificados.

articles.title: Depois do debate, quem entrou indeciso saiu ainda mais indeciso | G1
articles.body:
Depois do debate entre os candidatos à Presidência da República, o senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ) e o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), promovido pelo Grupo Bandeirantes, quem entrou indeciso saiu ainda mais indeciso.

Os dois candidatos travaram mais um embate de denúncias e acusações do que propriamente um debate de ideias. Elas até surgiram em meio ao pugilato, mas ficaram ofuscadas pela "guerrinha dos dois lados".

O resultado é que os bolsonaristas e os lulistas gostaram do desempenho do senador do PL e do presidente da República, mas quem estava indeciso, pelo visto, continuou indeciso.

Flávio Bolsonaro estava visivelmente mais bem preparado e disposto a provocar Lula para desestabilizá-lo. Já o presidente da República queria debater propostas e foi preparado para isso, mas acabou caindo na “pilha” do adversário ( leia mais abaixo ).

O risco para Flávio Bolsonaro é ter se mostrado arrogante e irônico demais. Esse estilo agrada ao seu eleitorado, com certeza, mas a tentativa de passar um ar de superioridade e maior domínio do palco não agradou aos eleitores indecisos.

Segundo o diretor da Ativa Datalab, Alek Maracajá, esse estilo transformou Lula em vítima e pode ter sensibilizado, de certa forma, o eleitor que ainda não decidiu seu voto e aquele que se absteve.

Maracajá ressalta, porém, que ainda não é possível garantir que isso vá se reverter em intenção de voto para o presidente. Ele reforça que também não é possível apontar um vencedor do debate de domingo (18) na Band.

Cada um animou sua plateia, mas a dúvida é como vai reagir o eleitor que ainda não decidiu. Pelos levantamentos da AtivaWeb DataLab, o indeciso permaneceu indeciso, mas pode ter ficado mais ao lado de Lula do que de Flávio Bolsonaro.

Na medição das menções nas redes sociais, Lula ficou à frente de Flávio Bolsonaro. Por outro lado, o candidato do PL conseguiu dominar o palco, mas também ficou acuado, principalmente quando o presidente fez perguntas incômodas ao senador, como as relacionadas à defesa de um homem que matou uma criança e à venda de munição sem registro.

O momento com maior número de visualizações foi o desafio feito por Lula para que ele e Flávio Bolsonaro abrissem seus sigilos bancários. O candidato do PL desconversou. Esse momento teve 10,2 milhões de visualizações.

Debate da Band entre Flávio Bolsonaro e Lula — Foto: Reuters/Jean Carniel

articles.title: Opinion - Accountability is coming: Trump aides face looming congressional probes
articles.summary: As the midterms approach, Congressional investigators are prepared to probe allegations of corruption and misconduct involving President Trump's appointees a...
articles.body:
The constant stream of crazy news stories coming out of the Trump administration is a bowl full of distractions, until a glance under the chaos reveals crass corruption.

Sixty percent of voters now rank "government corruption," as their top concern, according to a Fox News poll released last week . Corruption is a bigger issue than inflation or gas prices, with the midterm elections just days away. Exposure of the corruption will go beyond Election Day.

Congressional investigators will soon be asking how a Trump ambassador with access to national security information was revealed to have sent a "Honey Please," demand for money to a Trump donor.

Kimberly Guilfoyle, the ambassador to Greece, resigned after reports that she allegedly solicited $100,000 from the businessman to pay her personal credit card bill ahead of her Senate confirmation hearing, according to The Wall Street Journal .

Any ambassador with undisclosed financial obligations, as well as reported ties to dealmakers looking to profit from American investments overseas, is vulnerable to blackmail and extortion.

Congressional investigators, Republican or Democrat, might also ask how a former TV host and former girlfriend to the president's son, with no diplomatic experience, became an ambassador.

Government prosecutors have largely failed to hold Trump accountable for multiple charges of misconduct .

But as Trump's time in office expires, the people around him responsible for reckless and self-serving actions cannot assume they will have the same power to stay out of jail.

There will be a particularly hot congressional spotlight on several aides now representing Trump overseas. Did they mix the nation's global affairs and even the use of the American military with their personal business?

That list of high-flying Trump associates includes Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law. They have been largely free of scrutiny as the president's top foreign policy negotiators. But with Trump's hold on Congress fading in his last years in office, Witkoff and Kushner face increasing odds of being called for congressional testimony.

They will have to handle questions about their talks about billion-dollar oil refinery deals that "would benefit Middle Eastern business executives with ties..." to Witkoff and Kushner, according to reporting in last week's New York Times.

Also likely to have to testify under oath before Congress are the president's sons, Eric and Donald Trump Jr.

Both are heavily involved in cryptocurrency ventures, promoting an industry that has become a favored instrument for people skirting taxes and international sanctions law on business deals. Crypto is also a haven for hiding funds used by drug traffickers, and kidnappers. With Trump in office, his family has made billions from crypto .

Corporations have privately given Trump hundreds of millions for his ballroom project while several have government contracts, The Washington Post reported last week.

A former Trump aide likely to sit before Congress is the former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia. In her week on the job Zacharia stumbled in handling questions about her background and work in China. On television, she has repeatedly described herself as a lawyer. But journalists uncovered that she never practiced law in the U.S. The Wall Street Journal subsequently reported that she took the California bar exam and failed.

When reporters asked where she passed the bar, she offered an answer referring to her move to China. But foreign nationals cannot simply take the Chinese bar examination and become licensed Chinese lawyers. And her husband was involved with major business deals in China while she worked at a law firm in China.

Was that history uncovered in security-vetting process done by the White House?

Failure to properly report professional credentials and foreign ties is grounds for questioning. The government can't function with officials who can't be trusted with sensitive government information.

Last year, Joe Cirincione, a national security analyst, described the people Trump was nominating as ambassadors as "a diplomatic clown car that's about to be rolling up at the Capitol with all these idiots. ... Where's the outrage?" The outrage is now likely to emerge in congressional hearings.

Furious questioning is in store for Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. Another former television personality with no government experience, Hegseth has overseen American military strikes that killed people in the Caribbean. Videos of the attacks were released by Hegseth's team at the Pentagon. The administration described the targets as drug smugglers and made a spectacle of their deaths. But the evidence for using lethal U.S. military force against these alleged traffickers has never faced investigation by prosecutors or serious congressional scrutiny.

That was before Hegseth proposed showing the nation a livestreamed firing-squad execution of a man in a wheelchair . The White House later called off the barbaric display.

Using their subpoena power, congressional investigators need to prime the pump on reviewing financial disclosures, security-clearance applications and quid-pro-quo deals. They need to probe wasteful government contracts and the misuse of military force. Review of the financial dealings of presidential relatives and associates is overdue.

The records exist. The witnesses exist. Congress has the power to uncover the truth.

And the objective should be accountability, not political revenge. Polls show Americans, Republicans and Democrats, see the corruption. Accountability is coming. The diplomatic clown car is long overdue to be pulled over by police and the vehicle searched from tip-to-tail.

Juan Williams is senior political analyst for Fox News Channel and a prize-winning civil rights historian. He is the author of the new book " New Prize for These Eyes: The Rise of America's Second Civil Rights Movement . "

articles.title: ‘A warning sign for polling’: Why one GOP pollster thinks a blue wave may fall short
articles.summary: Echelon Insights’ Patrick Ruffini told POLITICO he thinks polling is overstating Democrats’ chances of flipping Senate races in historically deep-red territo...
articles.body:
Democrats are salivating over, and Republicans are bracing for, a potentially massive blue wave. One GOP pollster is urging everyone to calm down.

Patrick Ruffini, a founding partner at Echelon Insights, has been loudly throwing cold water on Democrats' hopes of sweeping the red state Senate seats that have become battlegrounds in a worsening national environment for Republicans.

"The polls are, I think, intentionally inflating the size of the battleground," Ruffini told POLITICO.

Democrats are pushing to flip Senate seats in Iowa, Texas, Ohio and Alaska — all states that President Donald Trump won by at least 11 points in 2024 — with dreams of going even deeper into the map Kansas, South Carolina and even Mississippi. Sensing a potential disaster, Republicans have significantly curtailed their investments in North Carolina and Georgia to direct resources elsewhere.

Ruffini, who isn't polling for candidates or party committees in any federal races, said he's skeptical of Democrats flipping some of those seats, particularly in the Midwest, and gives the GOP a coin flip's chance at keeping control of the Senate.

If a blue wave were to come, he said it would defy the ingrained partisanship in deep-red states that has mirrored growing political polarization around the country.

"I think it would be somewhat of a historic shift if that were to happen," he said.

Here's more from POLITICO's chat with Ruffini, edited for length and clarity. A more condensed version of this interview ran in POLITICO's Morning Score campaign newsletter.

You've been pretty publicly skeptical of polling that indicates a big tsunami for Democrats in November. Why is that?

I think we can read the environment right, but the map wrong.

The pretty large shift towards Democrats that we're seeing on the generic ballot and in a lot of individual races, I'm not saying that's not going to materialize. What I am more skeptical of is… the ability of any major party in this polarized era that we're in to rack up significant gains in states that went double digits for the other side.

I'm not ruling out — I think there will be some [examples]. I think Alaska is one where it's both an idiosyncratic state, and [Democratic nominee Mary] Peltola has shown some specific candidate-centered strength. Nor would it shock me if [Democrat] James Talarico wins, despite the history in Texas. That would not surprise me, just given the candidate quality disparity, particularly on the Ken Paxton side.

Where I get more skeptical is when you move into the Midwest, where there has historically been pretty large polling errors [overstating Democrats' chances] in states like Iowa, Ohio. And I think you can extend that to the Democratic enthusiasm around Kansas.

Is your skepticism coming more from the quality of the individual polls that you're seeing that are showing massive Democratic surges in the Midwest, or is it the history of these states that you're betting will ultimately win out?

I think fundamentals are going to play an important role, particularly in states where there was a solid Trump advantage. We're not talking about a state like North Carolina or Georgia that's only for Trump narrowly, where Democrats, at least in the Senate races, are clearly favored.

Historically the presumption is that states tend to converge on their base partisanship in the closing days of an election, but especially that's been the pattern in the Midwest.

Specifically as it relates to the polls this year, I think any pollster you would talk to, including myself, is experiencing significant non-response bias favoring Democrats.

When you're seeing high-propensity Democrats [responding to polls] at twice the rate of high-propensity Republicans, when we know that the turnout on both sides would be roughly evenly paired, that's a warning sign for polling in this cycle.

It seems like there's some GOP internal polling saying that Republicans are worried about these states, because they are moving money around to triage certain races . I'm curious if you feel like they're wrong to be making those decisions?

Absolutely not. They're not wrong. You do have to take the polls somewhat seriously in the sense of, if you do get a poll that's within the margin of error, I think you're duty-bound to spend money in those places and not to ignore what could be a potential signal.

I think that control of the Senate comes down to Texas, so they're right to be spending money there. If you just look at the amount of money being spent in Texas versus Kansas, obviously it's a much, much bigger state, and you need to spend much more money.

But it's not something along the lines of 'the battleground has shifted. It's a foregone conclusion. Democrats are going to win the Senate,' and then the battleground entirely shifts to a state like Kansas or to Iowa, right? I don't think we're seeing that.

It sounds like the issue you have is how the broader public is interpreting these polls rather than the polls themselves?

The polls are, I think, intentionally inflating the size of the battleground. And to some extent it's happening both ways. The polls showing a margin-of- error race in Minnesota is possible, right? I'm not as concerned about a polling error in Minnesota as I am in Kansas.

But because of the number of Democratic internals and because of the incentive of Democratic internals to show close races across the battleground, what you generally tend to see is more of an inflated sense of how big the battleground actually is. A lot of these races just break a certain way.

We've reported that Republicans are privately conceding that the House is lost. Is that your reading of the data too?

That's the best reading of the data. That said, if there's a three-point polling error or something, then I think it gets very, very tight and anything can happen. But I think that's the most likely outcome.

What is your prediction for the number of Senate seats Republicans will have?

My prediction for both the probability and the seat count is 50-50. There's a 50-50 chance Republicans hold the Senate. I think if they do, it's with 50 seats, probably. But obviously, that can tilt very easily.

Which of these states do you think are going to flip for Democrats?

Alaska is clearly favored. I mean, I don't know if it's clearly favored, but I think it's at least still Democrat. I think Texas is going to be very, very close. I just think the partisanship of the state is — people forget it's a little bit more Republican than it was back in 2018. I think Republicans are probably being underestimated in Ohio because of the past Midwestern polling error.

At the same time, I would say it's still uphill in Maine and Michigan to some degree. I think Susan Collins has really been the lone bright spot, at least in terms of the conventional wisdom, the narrative in the Senate for Republicans. I think she has a fighting chance, but I think Republicans are still probably under a 50% chance in both Michigan and Maine, just due to the nature of their partisan lean.

If at the end of all of this it is a real blue wave in the Senate, what will have happened to have made you wrong?

If that happens, we will have seen a level of depolarization in the electorate that we haven't seen since around 2012. You really have to go back in history for a state like Kansas to flip.That would be pretty unique historically, where it's a flip where you have an incumbent losing.

That's the kind of thing that used to happen in Senate races a lot, and then things, starting with Trump, got a lot more polarized. So what that would mean is, maybe this is the start of a new political era. But I think it would be somewhat of a historic shift if that were to happen.

articles.title: CNN’s Kaitlan Collins Claims Donald Trump Hired Katie Zacharia for One Reason
articles.summary: CNN’s Kaitlan Collins recently made a claim as to why Donald Trump hired Katie Zacharia as White House Press Secretary. Zacharia was announced to be taking o...
articles.body:
CNN's Kaitlan Collins recently made a claim as to why Donald Trump hired Katie Zacharia as White House Press Secretary. Zacharia was announced to be taking over the role in a post by Trump on Truth Social. However, she was fired after five days.

Kaitlan Collins describes Trump's reported dissatisfaction with Katie Zacharia's briefing

Kaitlan Collins from CNN recently took to X to share her thoughts on why Donald Trump might have hired Katie Zacharia as the new White House Press Secretary, only to then fire her days later.

Zacharia took over the role after Karoline Leavitt resigned in August 2026.

In her post, Collins suggested the President was "growing irritated" with how long the process to replace Leavitt was taking. She said Trump rushed to hire Zacharia as Press Secretary because he "wanted more people defending him on TV." According to the journalist, after a difficult first briefing, Trump allegedly believed Zacharia had failed at that task and "knew she needed to go."

Collins added, "I'm told Trump was embarrassed by the coverage of Zacharia's briefing and when he polled other aides about her, Zacharia had few allies willing to stand up for her or defend her performance."

In a post on October 12 on Truth Social , Trump announced Zacharia as the new White House Press Secretary. He mentioned that he believed she would do a "fantastic job" in her first briefing. However, Zacharia's first press interaction came under heavy scrutiny after she appeared to fumble parts of her speech.

A White House official later confirmed that Zacharia would leave the role after a rocky start. After firing her, Trump told reporters he asked Zacharia to reconsider the role because of how the press treated her. He said, "I told her, 'I think you're better off being happy.' I want her to have a good life. I don't want her to have a life like she's led the last three days" (via CBC ).

articles.title: Mass. Lt. Gov. candidate hit 5 parked cars and flipped SUV before arrest on OUI charge, police report says
articles.summary: Police say a former Massachusetts government lieutenant candidate was bleeding, glassy-eyed and smelled of alcohol after flipping his SUV on Dartmouth Street...
articles.body:
The former Massachusetts lieutenant governor-hopeful who was arrested in connection with drunken driving on Saturday night appeared in New Bedford court on Monday morning.

Shawn Oliver, 42, is facing charges of operating under the influence (OUI) of alcohol in addition to motor vehicles charges of negligent operation, marked lanes violation and speeding, according to charging documents in his case.

Oliver pleaded not guilty and was ordered released on personal recognizance from New Bedford District Court on Monday morning by Judge Joseph Harrington Jr. He is scheduled to appear again on Nov. 16.

Oliver is a current New Bedford city councilor and Bristol County House of Corrections officer who was running on the ticket as a Republican candidate with Mike Minogue against current Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll and Gov. Maura Healey. He announced he was suspending his campaign at around 2 p.m. on Sunday, less than 24 hours after his arrest Saturday night and after Minogue had called on him to do so Sunday morning.

"After careful reflection, I have made the decision to suspend my campaign for Lieutenant Governor," Oliver, who was running as a Republican in the race, said in a statement released at 2:17 p.m. on Sunday.

"This election is too important to be overshadowed by personal matters. I want to sincerely thank everyone who has supported me throughout this journey and ask that my family's privacy be respected during this difficult time," Oliver said.

Oliver's attorney could not immediately be reached for comment Monday.

According to three New Bedford police reports on the incident, Oliver was driving a black Lincoln Navigator north on Dartmouth Street at around 11:30 p.m., just south of the Rockdale Avenue intersection.

A witness who spoke to officers at the scene said he was stopped in his own car behind Oliver's Navigator at an intersection light on Dartmouth Street. When the light turned green, the witness said the Navigator did not pull forward.

After a few moments sitting at the light — and the witness reversing his own car to view that the light was green — the Navigator suddenly accelerated forward and drifted to the right, almost hitting the curb by New York Bagel at 571 Dartmouth St., the report read.

The Navigator then "abruptly" veered to the left to avoid striking the curb, the report read, and continued onward. After crossing through the Dartmouth and Rockdale intersection, the Navigator again drifted to the left and crossed over the yellow center line.

Police say Oliver struck five parked cars and was driving so fast that he flipped his Navigator upside down onto its roof.

Oliver was outside of the car and standing on the sidewalk, speaking on his cellphone when officers arrived at the scene, the report read. A bystander brought out a chair and officers told Oliver to sit down, noting that he was bleeding from an injury on the right side of his head.

Oliver repeatedly asked officers at the scene if "everyone else was OK," though they told him he was the only person involved in the crash, the report read. Oliver also told officers he was "burning both ends of the wick," and said he "was coming from a meeting with friends in Dartmouth."

Oliver was unable to complete a field sobriety test due to his injuries and was brought to the hospital, where he then told officers he'd drank at least two alcoholic beverages earlier in the night at Black Bass Grill. He then had gone to a friend's house located in Dartmouth, police said.

Oliver's eyes were "bloodshot and glassy," he was emanating "a moderate odor of alcoholic beverages" and he vomited at the hospital before he was placed under arrest.

"After speaking with Shawn, it was determined that he was under the influence of alcoholic beverages therefore should not have been operating a motor vehicle," the report read.

"At this point he was advised that he was being placed under arrest and was handcuffed to the hospital bed," the report read. Oliver refused to have his blood drawn at the hospital.

articles.title: Ro Khanna sparks backlash over France riot comments as critic says he wants to ‘ride the rage wave’
articles.summary: Ro Khanna argued France riots show a need to "listen to our young," drawing sharp backlash from critics who accused him of excusing political violence.
articles.body: Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., a potential 2028 presidential contender, drew criticism from across the political spectrum after pointing to the riots in France as a warning about wealth inequality and urging the U.S. to "listen to our young." "This is what happens when the nations let wealth and power accumulate in the hands of a few," Khanna wrote in a post to X on Sunday evening. Khanna's post comes on the heels of nationwide demonstrations over the cost of living and public services that descended into violence, looting and arson in several French cities on Saturday, prompting critics to accuse the progressive Democrat of giving political legitimacy to the destruction. Spencer Pratt, former mayoral candidate for Los Angeles, blasted what he saw as an attempt to side with rioters. JONATHAN TURLEY: SOCIALISM IS BACK IN STYLE AND DEMOCRATS ARE BUYING THE PITCH "Of course Rohit Conman sees mass communist riots destroying businesses and historic buildings in Paris and lies about it as some noble ‘ask’ for justice," Pratt wrote. "These commies lie as easily as they breathe." The comment also drew criticism from Shannon Watts, a Democratic gun activist who, in recent months, has criticized the far-left portions of her party. "If you’re a member of Congress who condemned the January 6 insurrection, you don’t get to excuse riots in France as a ‘cry for help.’ Political violence doesn’t become acceptable just because you sympathize with people committing it," Watts wrote in a post of her own. Still others warned Khanna against using the moment as a way to build political momentum. "Ro Khanna has long sought to ride the rage wave to power," Jonathan Turley, a political commentator and legal analyst, said. "Khanna could indeed learn much from France. This is history repeating itself. That history, by the way, does not bode well for establishment figures who pander to the mob," Turley added, giving a nod to the infamous French Revolution that targeted the country’s political and financial elite in a bloody crusade. Planned demonstrations in France over the weekend quickly spiraled out of control on Saturday, leaving behind broken storefronts and fires in Paris. French authorities said that by Sunday evening they had arrested nearly 2,400 people nationwide, including 855 in the Paris region. Nearly 1,000 police officers and gendarmes were injured, seven seriously, according to France's Interior Ministry. One protester died after suffering cardiac arrest during demonstrations in Paris, authorities said. WHERE'S MACRON? FRENCH LEADER BLASTED FOR ATTENDING CONCERT AS RIOTS ESCALATED In Limoges, a fire that authorities said was deliberately set at the city hall caused significant damage to the historic building. Shops were looted in Paris, Bordeaux, Marseille, Lyon and other cities, while public buildings were vandalized or targeted by fires. Authorities estimated that more than 550,000 people participated in demonstrations across France. Organizers put the figure at roughly 800,000. Despite the mayhem, Khanna argued the moment should prompt American lawmakers to take younger voters' political demands more seriously, especially on topics of equity. "This is what happens when young people lose hope in their future. In America, let us listen to our young. We need an economic and political transformation. America’s Next New Deal," Khanna wrote. "From the high schools of France to the streets of Madrid to the universities of Tirana, young people are telling their governments the same thing: in an age of massive wealth inequality, they want a future they can believe in," Khanna wrote. But in the face of the backlash online, Khanna quickly clarified his stance in a follow-up post, noting that he did not support the destruction that had unfolded. "I unequivocally condemn violence and vandalism. I have always championed my grandfather’s example of non-violent protest," Khanna wrote, referencing his relative, Amarnath Vidyalankar, who was imprisoned for advocating for India’s independence in the early 1930s. "Let us not be blind to the anger young people have against the unholy alliance of wealth and power. The billionaires buying politicians. The corruption," Khanna added. But even after issuing his clarifying statement, Khanna continued to face condemnation — even from figures like former Rep. George Santos, R-N.Y. "These are not mere students… my friend, I regret to inform you, this is an invasion," Santos wrote, referring to France’s high intake of refugees in recent years. Khanna, responding to Santos, doubled down on his view. BERNIE SANDERS ADMITS DEMOCRATS FAILED WORKING-CLASS VOTERS ON ECONOMICS, DRIVING THEM TO DONALD TRUMP "George, is the lesson not to tackle the vast disparity here and young people’s hopelessness?" he asked. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Khanna’s office did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Fox News Digital. Bradford Benz contributed to this report

articles.title: Trump threatened by judge with sanctions if he doesn’t sit for deposition in $10 billion BBC defamation suit
articles.summary: The BBC filed a motion to compel Donald Trump's deposition in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit, and a magistrate judge now warns of sanctions.
articles.body: President Donald Trump was threatened by a judge with sanctions if he doesn’t sit for a deposition in the $10 billion defamation lawsuit he filed against the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC). Trump filed a $10 billion lawsuit against the BBC late last year for its 2024 "Panorama" documentary that distorted his remarks to supporters on Jan. 6, 2021. Critics claim the documentary was misleading because it omitted Trump's call for supporters to protest peacefully, splicing together separate portions of a lengthy address to give a wrong impression. But Trump has been too busy to sit for a deposition, and the BBC said the president’s legal team insisted "has no availability whatsoever" before the end of the discovery period on Dec. 18 because he is busy dealing with "matters of national importance." TRUMP FILES 'POWERHOUSE' $10 BILLION LAWSUIT AGAINST BBC OVER DOCUMENTARY EDITING HIS JAN 6 REMARKS As a result, the BBC filed a motion to compel Trump’s deposition. The BBC has said it understands that Trump’s deposition requires "additional planning," and he "accepted the obligations of civil litigation" when he chose to file the lawsuit. "The Court has admonished Plaintiff for his lack of participation to no avail. Going forward, the Court expects strict compliance with its 29 Order, the failure of which will lead to sanctions," Magistrate Judge Enjolique A. Lett said on Friday, scheduling a hearing by Oct. 22. When asked for comment, Trump’s legal team blasted the British broadcaster. "The formerly respected and now disgraced BBC defamed President Trump by intentionally, maliciously, and deceptively doctoring his speech in a brazen attempt to interfere in the 2024 Presidential Election. The BBC has a long pattern of deceiving its audience in coverage of President Trump, all in service of its own leftist political agenda. President Trump’s powerhouse lawsuit is holding the BBC accountable for its defamation and reckless election interference just as he has held other fake news mainstream media responsible for their wrongdoing," a spokesperson for his legal team told Fox News Digital. LEGAL ANALYST PREDICTS TRUMP COULD WIN 'CONSIDERABLE' DAMAGES FROM BBC DOCUMENTARY LAWSUIT The BBC declined a request for comment. Trump filed the lawsuit against the BBC in December in a personal capacity for both defamation and for a violation of Florida’s Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act for $5 billion apiece, seeking $10 billion total. The documentary omitted Trump urging his supporters to protest "peacefully" and instead spliced two separate comments made nearly an hour apart, making him appear he was calling for violence. "We're going to walk down to the Capitol. And I'll be there with you. And we fight — we fight like hell," the documentary showed Trump saying. In reality, Trump said, "We're going to walk down to the Capitol. And we're going to cheer on our brave senators and congressmen and women, and we're probably not going to be cheering so much for some of them, because you'll never take back our country with weakness. You have to show strength, and you have to be strong." It wasn't until 54 minutes later that Trump called on his supporters to "fight like hell" for election integrity. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE The New York Times referred to the ordeal as "one of the worst crises in its 103-year history" of the BBC. The controversy led to the resignations of BBC News CEO Deborah Turness and BBC director-general Tim Davie. The BBC previously issued an apology for the erroneous edit and said it had pulled the program from its platforms. Despite the apology, the broadcaster has insisted the mistake is not enough for a defamation claim. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital’s Joseph A. Wulfson contributed to this report.

articles.title: DAQUI A POUCO: Debate na Globonews reúne coordenadores das campanhas de Flávio e Lula
articles.summary: DAQUI A POUCO: Debate na Globonews reúne coordenadores das campanhas de Flávio e Lula
articles.body:
O programa GloboNews Debate recebe, nesta segunda-feira (19), os coordenadores das campanhas de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) e Lula (PT). O g1 transmite ao vivo, nesta página.

Rogério Marinho, da campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro, e Edinho Silva, da equipe de Lula, vão discutir as estratégias para a reta final da eleição até o segundo turno, no próximo domingo (25).

A mediação é da jornalista Julia Duailibi. O programa começa às 18h20 e vai ao ar dentro do Edição das 18.

Rogério Marinho é senador pelo PL e um dos aliados mais próximos de Flávio Bolsonaro. Edinho Silva é presidente nacional do PT e deputado federal eleito, além de atuar na campanha de Lula.

Na reta final das eleições, o GloboNews Debate recebe os coordenadores das campanhas dos candidatos à Presidência Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) e Lula (PT).

Com mediação da jornalista Julia Duailibi, Rogério Marinho, coordenador da campanha do candidato do PL, e Edinho Silva, coordenador da campanha do candidato do PT, discutem as estratégias para o segundo turno.

articles.title: France's massive intel failure sparks resignation offers amid days of rioting
articles.summary: Emmanuel Macron ordered a security review after France's intelligence services badly underestimated protests that overwhelmed 60,000 police officers.
articles.body: France is confronting a major intelligence failure after authorities badly underestimated the scale of nationwide protests that descended into riots and looting. The days of chaos have prompted French President Emmanuel Macron to order a security review as senior officials acknowledged police "lost control" in several major cities and senior government officials have offered to resign after they failed to predict the level of pandemonium. Some 550,000 people joined 110 marches nationwide Saturday, according to France's Interior Ministry, far exceeding an intelligence estimate of roughly 200,000 demonstrators. Organizers put turnout even higher, at 800,000. Cars burned in the streets, more than 1,500 stores were reportedly ransacked or destroyed and public buildings were attacked across the country. In Limoges, rioters broke into and torched a 19th-century city hall that had survived both world wars, causing its roof to collapse. By Monday, the Louvre remained closed as student protesters blocked its entrances, extending the disruption into another day. TOP TOURIST DESTINATION IN THE WORLD SHUTS DOWN AMID VIOLENT PROTESTS The unrest overwhelmed some 60,000 police, gendarmes and other security personnel deployed nationwide. Nearly 1,000 law enforcement officers and firefighters were injured, at least 2,400 people were arrested and French authorities estimate some 3,000 businesses sustained damage. As crowds swelled, police were stretched across multiple flashpoints while groups of masked rioters smashed storefronts, set fires and clashed with security forces. In some cities, authorities were unable to keep looters from moving through commercial districts even as officers struggled to contain the larger demonstrations. By Monday, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez was acknowledging what shopkeepers and residents had already witnessed. FRENCH NEWSPAPER RIPS MACRON AFTER RIOTS ERUPT ACROSS FRANCE: ‘INDELIBLE STAIN’ "Yes, Saturday, in certain large cities, we lost control," Nuñez said. He acknowledged a "lack of anticipation" ahead of the demonstrations and said authorities had underestimated not only the number of protesters but the violent groups that would exploit the unrest. Nuñez offered his resignation to Macron. The president refused it and instead ordered a review of what the Élysée described as failures in planning and intelligence, demanding an accounting of how authorities had been caught so badly off guard. Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin was even more direct. "We unquestionably failed," Darmanin said, pointing specifically to intelligence and France's difficulty tracking and confronting the ultra-left. The failure is particularly striking because the unrest did not emerge without warning. The warning signs had been building for weeks. The unrest began in September with high school students protesting teacher shortages, deteriorating school buildings and other conditions in classrooms around Paris. The movement quickly spread nationwide, drawing teachers, labor unions and other groups frustrated by rising living costs and declining public services. Violence had already begun creeping into the demonstrations. Students set fires at schools, cars were torched and protesters clashed with riot police as authorities made thousands of arrests. French intelligence services were watching the shift. At an Oct. 1 government crisis meeting, intelligence officials assessed that the movement had reached a "tipping point" from school blockades toward urban violence and attributed its origins to the hard-left France Unbowed party and its allies, Reuters reported. Yet little more than two weeks later, authorities were caught off guard by the scale of what hit the streets. Saturday brought together students, trade unionists, Yellow Vest veterans and other groups under a loose "convergence of struggles." Hundreds of thousands marched peacefully, while smaller groups of masked rioters broke away, looting stores, setting fires and attacking police. The violence has since ignited a separate political fight over immigration. WHERE'S MACRON? FRENCH LEADER BLASTED FOR ATTENDING CONCERT AS RIOTS ESCALATED President Donald Trump blamed the destruction on France's migration policies, writing Monday that "the migrants have taken over France" and urging the country to close its borders. Other right-wing political leaders across Europe have made similar arguments. French authorities, however, have not blamed immigrants for the violence. Macron and his government have instead accused ultra-left militants and criminals of exploiting demonstrations rooted largely in education, living costs and public services. The unrest is nevertheless intensifying a political battle already reshaping France ahead of its 2027 presidential election, giving the right fresh ammunition on immigration, crime and the government's ability to maintain public order. Marine Le Pen's National Rally has seized on the violence to argue that Macron's government has lost control of the country, while other figures on the French right have pushed for tougher policing and immigration restrictions. The images of burning buildings, ransacked stores and overwhelmed police are landing at a particularly vulnerable moment for France's political establishment. Macron cannot seek a third consecutive term in 2027, leaving an open presidential contest as voters increasingly identify immigration, security and purchasing power among the country's major political concerns. The riots have also widened a debate over whether the breakdown reflects a failure of policing, deeper economic and social grievances or years of government policy on immigration and integration — competing explanations that are likely to shape France's political fight long after the streets are cleared. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP For Macron's government, the immediate question is more concrete: how security services that were already tracking an increasingly volatile protest movement still failed to anticipate the scale of Saturday's violence.
